cards.f: Path of air through the breathing system
cards.b: Nose/mouth → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (surrounded by capillaries).

cards.f: Four features of a gas exchange surface
cards.b: Large surface area, thin surface, good blood supply, good ventilation with air.

cards.f: Composition of inspired versus expired air
cards.b: Inspired: O₂ about 21%, CO₂ about 0.04%, less water vapour. Expired: O₂ about 16%, CO₂ about 4%, more water vapour.

cards.f: Why does expired air have more water vapour?
cards.b: Water evaporates from the moist lining of the alveoli.
Limewater turns from colourless to milky / cloudy.
Rate (breaths per minute) and depth (volume per breath) both increase.

cards.f: Explain why breathing speeds up during exercise
cards.b: More CO₂ made, so CO₂ in the blood rises; the brain detects this and causes faster, deeper breathing.

cards.f: Is respiration the same as breathing?
cards.b: No. Respiration is chemical reactions in all living cells releasing energy; breathing is ventilation of the lungs.

cards.f: Uses of energy in living organisms
cards.b: Muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, growth, nerve impulses, keeping body temperature constant.
Reactions in cells using oxygen to break down nutrient molecules and release energy. Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

cards.f: Define anaerobic respiration and give the muscle equation
cards.b: Reactions releasing energy without oxygen. In muscles: glucose → lactic acid. Releases much less energy per glucose.
Oxygen needed after vigorous exercise to deal with the lactic acid built up in muscles and blood.

cards.f: How is the oxygen debt removed after exercise?
cards.b: Fast heart rate carries lactic acid to the liver; deeper, faster breathing supplies oxygen; lactic acid is respired aerobically in the liver.

cards.f: Hydrogencarbonate indicator in a tube of germinating seeds
cards.b: Turns from red/orange to yellow, because respiration produces CO₂. Control: dead (boiled) seeds.

short.q: Explain how the alveoli are adapted for gas exchange. [3]
short.model: There are millions of alveoli giving a large surface area; walls are one cell thick for a short diffusion distance; a dense capillary network keeps a steep concentration gradient.
points: good blood supply maintains concentration gradient

short.q: Explain why expired air contains more carbon dioxide than inspired air. [2]
short.model: Cells produce carbon dioxide in respiration, which diffuses into the blood and then from the blood into the alveoli.

short.q: Explain why breathing rate stays high for some time after vigorous exercise. [3]
short.model: Anaerobic respiration made lactic acid and caused an oxygen debt; extra oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration of lactic acid in the liver.
points: for aerobic respiration of lactic acid in the liver

short.q: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscles. [2]
short.model: Aerobic uses oxygen and releases much more energy, producing CO₂ and water; anaerobic uses no oxygen and produces lactic acid.
points: products differ (CO₂ and water versus lactic acid)

short.q: Describe how you could show that expired air contains more carbon dioxide than inspired air. [3]
short.model: Breathe in through one tube of limewater and out through another; the limewater with expired air turns milky faster.
points: one for inspired air, one for expired air
expired air turns limewater milky faster
